passage: Sharmila had cut her list of rules to three, printed them and stuck them on her monitor. One said: if I finish lunch, then I plan tomorrow's top task. But meetings ran all afternoon that fortnight, and by Thursday the lunch rule had been ignored four days in a row. She noticed it and did not scold herself. Lunch always ended with a call rolling straight in. But at four she always shut her laptop. So on Friday she rewrote the rule: if I close my laptop at four, then I write down tomorrow's top task. Uday, at the next desk, saw the new sticky note and raised an eyebrow. "Same rule, different trigger," she said. On Monday the task was already written.

qa.a: Sharmila cut her list of rules to three.

qa.a: Sharmila could find another steady moment, such as leaving the desk for the day, or set a phone alarm at four to prompt the step.

qa.q: How might Uday see the new sticky note?

Sunaina's old plan had had twenty-four rules. By March she had cut it to three, written on a card taped beside her laptop in the Chandigarh office:
If a new request comes in, then ask for the deadline before saying yes.
If a meeting has no agenda, then ask for one.
After lunch, then clear the inbox for twenty minutes.
The first two worked. The third never happened. Every day after lunch, her colleague Bhupen came by to chat, or a call started, and the inbox stayed full.
On Friday she looked at the card and thought about when her day really slowed down. It was four o'clock, when the calls ended and she shut her laptop to stretch.
She crossed out "After lunch" and wrote "When I close my laptop at four".
The next week, she cleared the inbox four days out of five.

qa.q: How many days did Sunaina clear the inbox the next week?
qa.a: She cleared the inbox four days out of five.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt noticing the after-lunch rule never happened?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated at first, then thoughtful, looking for a better moment instead of blaming herself.

qa.q: Why was moving the trigger better than trying harder after lunch?
qa.a: Because after lunch was always interrupted, while closing the laptop at four is a calm moment that happens every day.

qa.q: How might Bhupen be affected by the change?
qa.a: Bhupen can still chat after lunch without spoiling Sunaina's plan, since the inbox time has moved to four.

grounding: It shows a woman keeping three if-then rules, noticing the after-lunch one is ignored, and moving its trigger to closing her laptop at four.

"Only three rules now?" Urmila asked, reading the sticky note on her sister's monitor.
"I had fifteen and remembered none," Payal said. "So: if someone asks for something urgent, I ask when they really need it. If I finish a call, I write one line of notes. And after lunch, I plan tomorrow."
"And do you?"
Payal sighed. "The first two, yes. Plan tomorrow after lunch? Not once in two weeks. After lunch everyone pings me."
"So when is your day quiet?"
Payal thought. "Four o'clock. When the stand-up ends and I close my laptop to get tea."
"Then that's your trigger."
Payal peeled off the note and rewrote the third line: When I close my laptop at four, plan tomorrow.
A week later, Urmila saw a neat list for the next day on the desk. "Working?"
"Five days out of five," Payal grinned.

qa.q: When does Payal close her laptop to get tea?
qa.a: Four o'clock, when the stand-up ends.

qa.q: How did Payal feel admitting the after-lunch rule never worked?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a little defeated, sighing that she hadn't planned once in two weeks.

qa.q: What else could Payal check after a few weeks?
qa.a: She could look again at which rule is being skipped and move its trigger too, since a rule only works if its moment really happens.

qa.q: How does Urmila see her sister's new plan?
qa.a: Urmila is curious and helpful, and pleased to see the neat list a week later.

grounding: It shows a woman keeping three if-then rules, noticing the after-lunch one is ignored, and moving its trigger to closing her laptop at four.
